name: crosstool-ng
why: Building cross-compilation toolchains from scratch reveals how compilers, libcs, and targets are actually assembled.

brief.what_it_is: Crosstool-NG is a generator for cross toolchains, the set of compiler, assembler, linker and C library that builds code for a different target machine than the one it runs on. Per the homepage it supports many architectures and components and has a menuconfig-style interface for choosing them. The README says the toolchain it produces will compile, assemble and link the code being developed, and that some pieces, such as static libraries, can end up inside the resulting binaries. Its command is ct-ng, which the README says is actually a make(2) script underneath. The README does not spell out the exact inputs and outputs beyond this, so treat the specifics of the configuration step as coming from the homepage description only.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage calls it a versatile (cross) toolchain generator with a simple yet powerful menuconfig-style interface. The README's framing is that toolchains are an essential component of a software development project and that the project aims at building them.
brief.how_it_works: ct-ng is a make-driven script, and the README warns that ct-ng --help prints make's help instead, with no clean workaround. The install docs describe a working directory where you run ct-ng help, which suggests you configure and build from there. The docs index lists sections on configuring, building the toolchain, toolchain types and how a toolchain is constructed, but I did not open those pages, so I cannot describe the build mechanism beyond that.

brief.install_notes: Beyond a package manager install, the docs say to first install extra host OS packages, since not all dependencies are detected by the configure script and missing ones may later make ct-ng build fail; the docs link per-distro instructions. You can use a released tarball (bz2 or xz, with PGP signatures from named maintainers since 1.21.0) or clone the git repo, which needs ./bootstrap before configure. You can either install it and discard the sources, or run it from the source directory with --enable-local, in which case the sources must be kept. Install creates a working directory for builds, and a man page for ct-ng is installed. Bash completion is not installed automatically; you copy bash-completion/ct-ng system-wide or per user.
brief.standout: The fact that ct-ng is a make script, so asking it for --help gets you make's help, is a memorable quirk the README flags openly. The project also documents its own install paths for running from a source tree, which suits people who want to hack on the toolchain builder itself.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage news lists a release of 1.29.0 dated Aug 23, 2026, with a 1.28.0 release dated Sep 6, 2025 further down, so the dates on the page are not in order. The homepage also has an Aug 11, 2026 post about AI bots hitting its web infrastructure. I did not check commit dates or the release page, so 'maintained' rests on the news items.
brief.caveats: The README warns that ct-ng --help shows make's help, not crosstool-NG's own. Not all host dependencies are detected by configure, so ct-ng build can fail later. Old Mercurial repositories are read-only. Contributed code in contrib/ is unmerged and comes with no guarantee it applies or works. The README says bug reports lacking required information get closed without explanation. I did not find the license in the pages I read. The install docs are Linux-oriented and link per-distro setup, but I did not check other platforms.
quotes: Crosstool-NG is a versatile (cross) toolchain generator.
It supports many architectures and components and has a simple yet powerful menuconfig-style interface.
Note: If you call `ct-ng --help` you will get help for `make(2)`. This is because ct-ng is in fact a `make(2)` script. There is no clean workaround for this.
